Cagey Cajees

By: Kate Barry | Commission

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We bring you the real story of the Africrypt rug-pull, and what happened to the brazen brothers who pulled off South Africa's biggest Bitcoin heist.

Unique Selling Point:
Interviews with two associates who met Raees and Ameer Cajee in Dubai after their escape from South Africa, helped them relocate and set up residence and introduced them to new clients.
We find out how they skipped the country in a hurry, where they lived, where they partied, where they holidayed, what they spent their investors' money on. And ultimately, how they stole another $10 million in a second rug pull before relocating back to South Africa .

Summary:
It was the cyber heist of the century. R3 billion in Bitcoin disappeared overnight in April 2021. The Africrypt whizz kids Raees & Ameer Cajee claimed they were hacked, but by then they were living comfortably in Dubai with Vanuatu passports. It later emerged that amount stolen was closer to $10 million.
Desperate investors hired lawyers and liquidators tp pursue criminal charges. Then an angel investor appeared on the scene - Pennython Project Management from Dubai offered to refund the investors 70 cents in the Rand, on condition that all criminal charges were dropped. 95% of the investors took the deal. But in the interim the Cajee brothers profited hugely on Bitcoin that had increased dramatically in value.
In a dramatic Dubai kidnapping, Bilal Cajee, father of Raees and Ameer was snatched while visiting the Dubai court. When the brothers finally went to the police they pinged his phone. Bilal was found in the Millennium Hotel near the Dubai airport, tied to a chair in a hotel room. The brothers were tight-lipped, but it is believed a disgruntled South African investor had held him captive until the Cajees repaid what they'd stolen.
In late 2021 Ameer Cajee was arrested in Zurich when he tried to stash a Trezor stick, containing the stolen Bitcoin, in a Swiss bank vault. Accused of money laundering he spent 6 months in a Swiss detention centre. Once Pennython had paid out the South African clients, they agreed to release him on CHF 300 000 bail. He spent another year under house arrest in the Five Hotel, in the luxurious $1000 a night penthouse.
In the interim his brother organised a second Vanuatu passport for him. When the Swiss authorities released him, they flew back to South Africa on Turkish airlines, via Istanbul.


Further information:
The Cajee brothers have now stolen $10 million in crypto currency from their Dubai investors, and are hiding out in South Africa. The NPA refuse to pursue criminal charges as the crime was committed in the UAE. The brothers are believed to be resident in Zimbali Estate in KZN and in Johannesburg. They currently have just over $100 million in their crypto wallet, and the Dubai investors are pursuing a civil claim against them.
Shaheed Dollie, the Cajee's lawyer has reneged on meeting set up with the claimants' lawyer, Gerhard Botha.
These two youngsters continue to profit off their ill-gotten gains, repeating the same pattern - rug-pull, disappear, then offer to settle an keep the profits.

CAGEY CAJEES 4

V/O: Dubai…the city of dreams.

After the Covid-19 lockdown, a fund manager - who we’ll call Michael - moved to the Middle East looking for new opportunities in this global business hub. He attended a networking lunch at the Drift Beach Club, where he got talking to two brothers.

Michael: So, I met the brothers in December 2020. I think it took about 5 minutes before we started talking about cryptocurrency and digital assets. And I had been managing digital assets for a few years at that stage, and they obviously had been as well. And I could obviously tell that they knew what they were talking about and had a great understanding of the industry in general.

V/O: They exchanged numbers and the crypto-enthusiasts became good friends.

Michael: We would often meet up face to face, multiple times a week, talking about digital assets, trading digital assets, talking about the ecosystem, what we think will happen with regulation.

V/O: But why should we care about this new friendship in a foreign country? Well, Michael’s new crypto chums were South Africans…soon to be infamous.

Link: Michael may have hit it off with them, but little did he know that these two South African youngsters were hiding a dirty secret.

V/O: 20-year-old Raees Cajee and his 18-year-old brother Ameer were planning Africa’s biggest crypto scam. In April 2021 they claimed their digital investment platform Africrypt had been hacked. Investors lost an estimated R700 million in Bitcoin - a digital currency that operates without a central bank, allowing online transactions with no government oversight.

Reports of a $3.6 billion loss were exaggerated, but the so-called hack turned out to be a heist, and the brothers vanished overnight.
But we now know their exit scam was planned months in advance.

Jerry: They were introduced to us by an existing client from Johannesburg in South Africa. And they told us they were interested in acquiring second citizenship.

V/O: This man is an immigration consultant we’ll call Jerry. The brothers contacted him seven months before the heist asking for Vanuatu citizenship.

Jerry: Vanuatu is not perhaps a very well-known country. But it’s on the other side of the world between Australia and New Zealand. It’s a former Commonwealth country, and at the time of application it had visa-free access to all of Europe and to the UK.

Lourensa: Did anything strike you as unusual about this application?

Jerry: There was nothing unusual except they seemed to be in a hurry. One of the reasons why they chose Vanuatu - it was a very, very quick process to get a passport. 60 to 70 days you could be a citizen. They said that they had no bank accounts anywhere and that all their money was in crypto, and that they wouldn’t be able to provide bank statements. And the only assets they had was a very large car collection

V/O: However, Raees and Ameer were granted citizenship and collected their new passports at Jerry’s office in Dubai.

Jerry: They were extremely polite. They were seemingly very intelligent. So, they were quite easy to get on with.

V/O: The Cajees invited Jerry to lunch with a business proposal.

Jerry: And they said look; we’re interested in developing the board of Africrypt and specifically having – to use their words – white-faced Europeans as the front of the company because we think we would be able to generate more investment and bring more money into the funds, and we would like to sit in the background and be the traders.
Jerry: I’m delighted I said no.

Lourensa: Do you think that they were trying to set you up?

Jerry: I think they knew what they were planning. Yeah, they were definitely looking for front-facing CEOs to take the fall.

V/O: Instead, he helped them register a company in Dubai, and residency permits for the whole family were issued in late April. But Jerry knew nothing of the Africrypt drama unfolding in South Africa.

Jerry: They called me urgently one evening and said that they had to speed up the process extremely urgently because they had received death threats in Johannesburg and they wanted to move to Dubai with immediate effect.
And then they couldn’t fly direct because of the Covid situation.
And they said we’re going to fly and stop somewhere in between for 14 days.

Lourensa: The Cajee brothers left Joburg in a hurry - boarding a plane to the Maldives with their whole family. But what were they running from? Were their lives really in danger, or were they simply escaping with their clients’ assets? Or both?

Michael: They moved to a villa outside the city centre and they had security. And I would go and visit them at their villa, and their villa was absolutely incredible. I think the rent was a million dirhams a year, that’s about $250 000 a year. It was a beautiful multi-bedroom villa. They had Rolls Royces that were worth $150 000, $200 000. At one stage Raees wanted to give himself a nice birthday gift and he imported a very rare Porsche from the United States into Dubai. Their villa had a turntable where you could put a car on the turntable and have it spin around.

V/O: This classic Lamborghini Countach is worth $600 000.

Jerry : They liked to go to the gold and diamond souk here. So, they would always turn up in very nice new watches or diamond chains, gold chains, etc. etc. They frequented the best restaurants in town. They used to go to a lot of the nightclubs and a few of the party establishments over here. So, they had the lifestyle of very wealthy 21, 22-year-olds.

V/O: Michael was so impressed with their trading expertise that he agreed to start a crypto fund with them – a decision that would cost him dearly. It was the start of the alleged second heist.

Michael: It was about May 2021 when we decided it might be a great idea for us to do business together. They were excellent traders, and I thought I could be very good with client management.

V/O: And so, in blissful ignorance, he started raising investment capital for two scammers, and millions of dollars started rolling in. The Africrypt heist was big news in South Africa, but it took two months to break internationally. Michael read about it on Bloomberg News.

Michael: I confronted them and said Hey guys, like what the hell is going on? I didn’t know it was a rug pull. They were telling everyone here in Dubai that they were hacked.

V/O: They insisted Africrypt was robbed by a third party.

Michael: So, I felt bad for them. And I was saying look guys, if you have actually been hacked, find the right people to prove the hack and get out ahead of it. But they had a lot of sympathy here in Dubai in the early days because they had convincingly sold the fact that they had been hacked.

V/O: But forensic analysis proved the security breach was an inside job.

Michael: The lies were unbelievable in hindsight.

Lourensa: Imagine being a teenager with access to millions of dollars in Bitcoin? Magnificent mansions, exotic cars, glamorous holidays – and not in cattle class like the rest of us - everything was First Class. It’s easy to see why they wouldn’t want to give that up.

V/O: The Cajees deposited crypto wallets with millions of dollars in digital assets in a Swiss bank vault. But when Ameer returned to Zurich, he was arrested on suspicion of money laundering.

V/O: With criminal charges pending in South Africa, he spent six months in prison, before being released on bail. A suite at the luxurious Five Hotel in Zurich was his home for the next nine months while under house arrest.

Michael: I went to go see him at the Five Hotel in Zurich and I asked a lot of hard questions. And he basically said they were still trying to prove the hack and that this whole thing was a big mistake.

V/O: Ameer wasn’t permitted to leave Switzerland until the South African investors were compensated. Attorney Gerhard Botha represented many of them.

Botha: They had to prove their claims to the liquidator, and then a new investor from Dubai bought those claims.

V/O: In other words, the Cajees sold the debt and were off the hook. The mystery investor was Pennython Project Management, registered in Dubai.

Botha: At the end of the day, I think the Cajee brothers basically just managed the process.

V/O: The liquidation settlement was R200 million. Individual investors got 65 cents in the Rand in exchange for dropping criminal charges against the Cajees.

Lourensa: During your visits, did it seem as though Ameer was concerned at all? Did he show any remorse?

Michael: There wasn't a lot of remorse, and I thought it was because they were hacked, but it actually was just their... that was just who they are. I mean, these two are stone cold criminals. They're career criminals. They have no empathy. They have no remorse. They don't care about anyone but themselves. And I think that's the thing that I've realized since my own theft.

V/O: Throughout Ameer’s detention Michael continued trading with the Cajees, investing $5 million in digital assets.

Link: With all the bad press out there, it’s difficult to understand why investors in Dubai would still trust the Cajees with their money. But the cash kept coming, and oops, it disappeared again!

V/O: Just before the crypto collapse in 2022, Michael decided to take his assets off the online exchanges and put them on cold storage devices for safeguarding. These wallets hold the unique codes or passwords to manage and spend funds.

Michael: But the key thing about the cold storage is you have to have custody of the cold storage device in order to trade. And I had left the cold storage devices with Raees as I was travelling a lot internationally and did not want to bring them with me. And that is when the misappropriation of assets, the falsified trading data, and eventually the theft and them starting to ghost me – that’s when that all began to happen.

V/O: Eventually, in February 2023 Ameer was allowed to leave Switzerland.

Michael: I expected Ameer to come back to Dubai, but he went back to South Africa. And then just like that, overnight, the whole family was gone. The villa was empty, and I haven’t talked to them since.

Lourensa: So, they disappeared and your money disappeared. How much money did you lose?

Michael: So, if my assets were being managed properly today, the way we were back in 2021 and 2022, it would be around 50 million US dollars.

Lourensa: That’s a lot of money.

Michael: It’s a terrifying amount of money to lose.

Lourensa: What does that mean for you financially?

Michael: Oh, it’s completely destroyed me.
.
V/O: Michael has engaged Botha to try and get his money back.

Botha: In Dubai criminal charges have been laid, so there is an investigation ongoing in Dubai. In South Africa we are tracing the Cajees. We have issued summons; we’ve tried to serve summons unsuccessfully.

V/O: A registered address of the Cajees is the exclusive Zimbali Estate north of Durban. But these mansions enjoy excellent security and we couldn’t gain access.

Botha: They can protect themselves. They’ve got security, because they have money.

V/O: But then we received a tipoff that the Cajees were enjoying the festive season in KZN’s premier holiday destination.

Link: So, they’ve recently been spotted here at The Pearls in Umhlanga Rocks. To be honest, we’re not even sure if they’re still around or in which apartment they’re staying, but we’re going to try and track them down.

V/O: But it seems they’d already left, so we went to another province.

Lourensa: This is a recent address for the Cajees in Johannesburg. The Sheriff tried to serve summons here but couldn’t find them. They say the early bird catches the worm… maybe we’ll have more luck.

Lourensa: Unit Number 2? You don’t know them? Okay, so they’re not here.

V/O: Repeated requests to the Cajee brothers for an interview were ignored, as were the questions we sent asking for written comment.

Michael: And let me just say that this is absolutely their modus operandi. Their business is to gain people’s trust, steal their money and then disappear. And then eventually they will probably negotiate some kind of settlement. And in the meantime, they will have traded those assets, made an absolute fortune on them, leaving people who have burned by them in financial ruin.

Lourensa: Will you accept a settlement?

Michael: I would accept a settlement in some way, shape or form. But eventually, I think they need to end up behind bars. Because even if I do recover my assets plus damages, they’re not going to stop. I don’t see them ever stopping. It’s very important to understand that they’re professional liars and they’re professional conmen.

Lourensa: So, to be clear, you want to see them locked up?

Michael: I would love to see them in jail for the rest of their lives, absolutely. That would be a dream come true.

Insert in Show: Title Author Last Updated 15 February 2026 - Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 16 February 2026 TX Date: 0000-00-00 Script: CAGEY CAJEES 4 V/O: Dubai…the city of dreams. After the Covid-19 lockdown, a fund manager - who we’ll call Michael - moved to the Middle East looking for new opportunities in this global business hub. He attended a networking lunch at the Drift Beach Club, where he got talking to two brothers. Michael: So, I met the brothers in December 2020. I think it took about 5 minutes before we started talking about cryptocurrency and digital assets. And I had been managing digital assets for a few years at that stage, and they obviously had been as well. And I could obviously tell that they knew what they were talking about and had a great understanding of the industry in general. V/O: They exchanged numbers and the crypto-enthusiasts became good friends. Michael: We would often meet up face to face, multiple times a week, talking about digital assets, trading digital assets, talking about the ecosystem, what we think will happen with regulation. V/O: But why should we care about this new friendship in a foreign country? Well, Michael’s new crypto chums were South Africans…soon to be infamous. Link: Michael may have hit it off with them, but little did he know that these two South African youngsters were hiding a dirty secret. V/O: 20-year-old Raees Cajee and his 18-year-old brother Ameer were planning Africa’s biggest crypto scam. In April 2021 they claimed their digital investment platform Africrypt had been hacked. Investors lost an estimated R700 million in Bitcoin - a digital currency that operates without a central bank, allowing online transactions with no government oversight. Reports of a $3.6 billion loss were exaggerated, but the so-called hack turned out to be a heist, and the brothers vanished overnight. But we now know their exit scam was planned months in advance. Jerry: They were introduced to us by an existing client from Johannesburg in South Africa. And they told us they were interested in acquiring second citizenship. V/O: This man is an immigration consultant we’ll call Jerry. The brothers contacted him seven months before the heist asking for Vanuatu citizenship. Jerry: Vanuatu is not perhaps a very well-known country. But it’s on the other side of the world between Australia and New Zealand. It’s a former Commonwealth country, and at the time of application it had visa-free access to all of Europe and to the UK. Lourensa: Did anything strike you as unusual about this application? Jerry: There was nothing unusual except they seemed to be in a hurry. One of the reasons why they chose Vanuatu - it was a very, very quick process to get a passport. 60 to 70 days you could be a citizen. They said that they had no bank accounts anywhere and that all their money was in crypto, and that they wouldn’t be able to provide bank statements. And the only assets they had was a very large car collection V/O: However, Raees and Ameer were granted citizenship and collected their new passports at Jerry’s office in Dubai. Jerry: They were extremely polite. They were seemingly very intelligent. So, they were quite easy to get on with. V/O: The Cajees invited Jerry to lunch with a business proposal. Jerry: And they said look; we’re interested in developing the board of Africrypt and specifically having – to use their words – white-faced Europeans as the front of the company because we think we would be able to generate more investment and bring more money into the funds, and we would like to sit in the background and be the traders. Jerry: I’m delighted I said no. Lourensa: Do you think that they were trying to set you up? Jerry: I think they knew what they were planning. Yeah, they were definitely looking for front-facing CEOs to take the fall. V/O: Instead, he helped them register a company in Dubai, and residency permits for the whole family were issued in late April. But Jerry knew nothing of the Africrypt drama unfolding in South Africa. Jerry: They called me urgently one evening and said that they had to speed up the process extremely urgently because they had received death threats in Johannesburg and they wanted to move to Dubai with immediate effect. And then they couldn’t fly direct because of the Covid situation. And they said we’re going to fly and stop somewhere in between for 14 days. Lourensa: The Cajee brothers left Joburg in a hurry - boarding a plane to the Maldives with their whole family. But what were they running from? Were their lives really in danger, or were they simply escaping with their clients’ assets? Or both? Michael: They moved to a villa outside the city centre and they had security. And I would go and visit them at their villa, and their villa was absolutely incredible. I think the rent was a million dirhams a year, that’s about $250 000 a year. It was a beautiful multi-bedroom villa. They had Rolls Royces that were worth $150 000, $200 000. At one stage Raees wanted to give himself a nice birthday gift and he imported a very rare Porsche from the United States into Dubai. Their villa had a turntable where you could put a car on the turntable and have it spin around. V/O: This classic Lamborghini Countach is worth $600 000. Jerry : They liked to go to the gold and diamond souk here. So, they would always turn up in very nice new watches or diamond chains, gold chains, etc. etc. They frequented the best restaurants in town. They used to go to a lot of the nightclubs and a few of the party establishments over here. So, they had the lifestyle of very wealthy 21, 22-year-olds. V/O: Michael was so impressed with their trading expertise that he agreed to start a crypto fund with them – a decision that would cost him dearly. It was the start of the alleged second heist. Michael: It was about May 2021 when we decided it might be a great idea for us to do business together. They were excellent traders, and I thought I could be very good with client management. V/O: And so, in blissful ignorance, he started raising investment capital for two scammers, and millions of dollars started rolling in. The Africrypt heist was big news in South Africa, but it took two months to break internationally. Michael read about it on Bloomberg News. Michael: I confronted them and said Hey guys, like what the hell is going on? I didn’t know it was a rug pull. They were telling everyone here in Dubai that they were hacked. V/O: They insisted Africrypt was robbed by a third party. Michael: So, I felt bad for them. And I was saying look guys, if you have actually been hacked, find the right people to prove the hack and get out ahead of it. But they had a lot of sympathy here in Dubai in the early days because they had convincingly sold the fact that they had been hacked. V/O: But forensic analysis proved the security breach was an inside job. Michael: The lies were unbelievable in hindsight. Lourensa: Imagine being a teenager with access to millions of dollars in Bitcoin? Magnificent mansions, exotic cars, glamorous holidays – and not in cattle class like the rest of us - everything was First Class. It’s easy to see why they wouldn’t want to give that up. V/O: The Cajees deposited crypto wallets with millions of dollars in digital assets in a Swiss bank vault. But when Ameer returned to Zurich, he was arrested on suspicion of money laundering. V/O: With criminal charges pending in South Africa, he spent six months in prison, before being released on bail. A suite at the luxurious Five Hotel in Zurich was his home for the next nine months while under house arrest. Michael: I went to go see him at the Five Hotel in Zurich and I asked a lot of hard questions. And he basically said they were still trying to prove the hack and that this whole thing was a big mistake. V/O: Ameer wasn’t permitted to leave Switzerland until the South African investors were compensated. Attorney Gerhard Botha represented many of them. Botha: They had to prove their claims to the liquidator, and then a new investor from Dubai bought those claims. V/O: In other words, the Cajees sold the debt and were off the hook. The mystery investor was Pennython Project Management, registered in Dubai. Botha: At the end of the day, I think the Cajee brothers basically just managed the process. V/O: The liquidation settlement was R200 million. Individual investors got 65 cents in the Rand in exchange for dropping criminal charges against the Cajees. Lourensa: During your visits, did it seem as though Ameer was concerned at all? Did he show any remorse? Michael: There wasn't a lot of remorse, and I thought it was because they were hacked, but it actually was just their... that was just who they are. I mean, these two are stone cold criminals. They're career criminals. They have no empathy. They have no remorse. They don't care about anyone but themselves. And I think that's the thing that I've realized since my own theft. V/O: Throughout Ameer’s detention Michael continued trading with the Cajees, investing $5 million in digital assets. Link: With all the bad press out there, it’s difficult to understand why investors in Dubai would still trust the Cajees with their money. But the cash kept coming, and oops, it disappeared again! V/O: Just before the crypto collapse in 2022, Michael decided to take his assets off the online exchanges and put them on cold storage devices for safeguarding. These wallets hold the unique codes or passwords to manage and spend funds. Michael: But the key thing about the cold storage is you have to have custody of the cold storage device in order to trade. And I had left the cold storage devices with Raees as I was travelling a lot internationally and did not want to bring them with me. And that is when the misappropriation of assets, the falsified trading data, and eventually the theft and them starting to ghost me – that’s when that all began to happen. V/O: Eventually, in February 2023 Ameer was allowed to leave Switzerland. Michael: I expected Ameer to come back to Dubai, but he went back to South Africa. And then just like that, overnight, the whole family was gone. The villa was empty, and I haven’t talked to them since. Lourensa: So, they disappeared and your money disappeared. How much money did you lose? Michael: So, if my assets were being managed properly today, the way we were back in 2021 and 2022, it would be around 50 million US dollars. Lourensa: That’s a lot of money. Michael: It’s a terrifying amount of money to lose. Lourensa: What does that mean for you financially? Michael: Oh, it’s completely destroyed me. . V/O: Michael has engaged Botha to try and get his money back. Botha: In Dubai criminal charges have been laid, so there is an investigation ongoing in Dubai. In South Africa we are tracing the Cajees. We have issued summons; we’ve tried to serve summons unsuccessfully. V/O: A registered address of the Cajees is the exclusive Zimbali Estate north of Durban. But these mansions enjoy excellent security and we couldn’t gain access. Botha: They can protect themselves. They’ve got security, because they have money. V/O: But then we received a tipoff that the Cajees were enjoying the festive season in KZN’s premier holiday destination. Link: So, they’ve recently been spotted here at The Pearls in Umhlanga Rocks. To be honest, we’re not even sure if they’re still around or in which apartment they’re staying, but we’re going to try and track them down. V/O: But it seems they’d already left, so we went to another province. Lourensa: This is a recent address for the Cajees in Johannesburg. The Sheriff tried to serve summons here but couldn’t find them. They say the early bird catches the worm… maybe we’ll have more luck. Lourensa: Unit Number 2? You don’t know them? Okay, so they’re not here. V/O: Repeated requests to the Cajee brothers for an interview were ignored, as were the questions we sent asking for written comment. Michael: And let me just say that this is absolutely their modus operandi. Their business is to gain people’s trust, steal their money and then disappear. And then eventually they will probably negotiate some kind of settlement. And in the meantime, they will have traded those assets, made an absolute fortune on them, leaving people who have burned by them in financial ruin. Lourensa: Will you accept a settlement? Michael: I would accept a settlement in some way, shape or form. But eventually, I think they need to end up behind bars. Because even if I do recover my assets plus damages, they’re not going to stop. I don’t see them ever stopping. It’s very important to understand that they’re professional liars and they’re professional conmen. Lourensa: So, to be clear, you want to see them locked up? Michael: I would love to see them in jail for the rest of their lives, absolutely. That would be a dream come true.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We bring you the real story of the Africrypt rug-pull, and what happened to the brazen brothers who pulled off South Africa's biggest Bitcoin heist.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Interviews with two associates who met Raees and Ameer Cajee in Dubai after their escape from South Africa, helped them relocate and set up residence and introduced them to new clients. We find out how they skipped the country in a hurry, where they lived, where they partied, where they holidayed, what they spent their investors' money on. And ultimately, how they stole another $10 million in a second rug pull before relocating back to South Africa .
metadata.Summary: It was the cyber heist of the century. R3 billion in Bitcoin disappeared overnight in April 2021. The Africrypt whizz kids Raees & Ameer Cajee claimed they were hacked, but by then they were living comfortably in Dubai with Vanuatu passports. It later emerged that amount stolen was closer to $10 million. Desperate investors hired lawyers and liquidators tp pursue criminal charges. Then an angel investor appeared on the scene - Pennython Project Management from Dubai offered to refund the investors 70 cents in the Rand, on condition that all criminal charges were dropped. 95% of the investors took the deal. But in the interim the Cajee brothers profited hugely on Bitcoin that had increased dramatically in value. In a dramatic Dubai kidnapping, Bilal Cajee, father of Raees and Ameer was snatched while visiting the Dubai court. When the brothers finally went to the police they pinged his phone. Bilal was found in the Millennium Hotel near the Dubai airport, tied to a chair in a hotel room. The brothers were tight-lipped, but it is believed a disgruntled South African investor had held him captive until the Cajees repaid what they'd stolen. In late 2021 Ameer Cajee was arrested in Zurich when he tried to stash a Trezor stick, containing the stolen Bitcoin, in a Swiss bank vault. Accused of money laundering he spent 6 months in a Swiss detention centre. Once Pennython had paid out the South African clients, they agreed to release him on CHF 300 000 bail. He spent another year under house arrest in the Five Hotel, in the luxurious $1000 a night penthouse. In the interim his brother organised a second Vanuatu passport for him. When the Swiss authorities released him, they flew back to South Africa on Turkish airlines, via Istanbul.
metadata.Further information: The Cajee brothers have now stolen $10 million in crypto currency from their Dubai investors, and are hiding out in South Africa. The NPA refuse to pursue criminal charges as the crime was committed in the UAE. The brothers are believed to be resident in Zimbali Estate in KZN and in Johannesburg. They currently have just over $100 million in their crypto wallet, and the Dubai investors are pursuing a civil claim against them. Shaheed Dollie, the Cajee's lawyer has reneged on meeting set up with the claimants' lawyer, Gerhard Botha. These two youngsters continue to profit off their ill-gotten gains, repeating the same pattern - rug-pull, disappear, then offer to settle an keep the profits.
